track.name: sales
track.label: B2B Sales
track.summary: Learn the core playbook of B2B sales — prospecting, qualifying, discovery, presenting, objection handling, closing, and account management — the practical skills every sales or customer-facing role assumes.

phases.title: Sales Fundamentals & the Buyer's Journey
phases.description: Understand how modern B2B buyers research and decide, and the inbound philosophy that shapes how good salespeople sell today.

phases.title: Prospecting & Qualifying
phases.description: Fill the pipeline with the right prospects, reach them without getting ignored, and use frameworks like BANT and MEDDIC to judge what's actually worth pursuing.

phases.title: Discovery & Needs Analysis
phases.description: Run discovery calls that surface a buyer's real problems, using active listening and structured questioning like SPIN.

phases.title: Presenting & Handling Objections
phases.description: Deliver demos and pitches that connect to real value, and handle the objections that come up before a deal can close.

phases.title: Closing & Negotiation
phases.description: Move a qualified opportunity to a signed deal — closing techniques, negotiation fundamentals, and keeping a pipeline honest in a CRM.

phases.title: Account Management & Customer Success
phases.description: Turn a closed deal into a lasting account — renewals, relationship management, and growing revenue from existing customers.

topics.title: Intro to B2B Sales & the Modern Buyer's Journey
topics.description: How B2B buyers move from awareness to decision, and why most of that journey now happens before they ever talk to a salesperson.

steps.t: Map the modern B2B buyer's journey
steps.d: Interview three B2B customers and document at least five milestones they hit before they ever spoke to a salesperson (research, comparison, etc.).
Ask those same customers what sources they trusted most and what convinced them to take a call (articles, referrals, product tours).
Document your current sales process (where you touch prospects, what you ask in discovery) and identify gaps where customers are already deciding before you engage.
Define the stages a prospect moves through in their buying journey and the buying signal that indicates movement to the next stage.
Write down the first place in your sales process where you're asking for something the buyer hasn't decided yet.

topics.title: The Inbound Sales Methodology
topics.description: Sell in a way that matches how buyers already research and buy, instead of running a generic, one-size-fits-all pitch.

steps.d: Review how inbound sales works: attracting buyers to you instead of interrupting them, and aligning your process with how they already buy.
Categorize your last ten outreach touches as either inbound (resource, invite to event, insight) or outbound (cold call, generic email), and count each type.
Interview five prospects who didn't buy and write down the top three reasons they were hesitant or passed.
Take your first-touch outreach and rewrite it so it leads with insight or value instead of a pitch, and increases reply rate (test with five people).
After one month of inbound-aligned touches, compare reply rate and qualification rate to your previous month's data.

topics.title: Prospecting Fundamentals
topics.description: Build a repeatable process for finding and reaching the right prospects instead of relying on random outreach.

steps.d: Document the five most important characteristics of your best customers (company size, industry, pain point, revenue, geography).
Using your ICP, create a list of 50-100 companies that match your profile and research at least ten of them (what they do, who leads, what they might need).
For five companies on your list, find the actual name and title of the person (or people) who would decide to buy your product.
Commit to prospecting ten new accounts per week and document how you'll reach them (email, phone, LinkedIn, referral request).
After four weeks, count how many prospects you reached, how many replied, and how many moved to a discovery conversation.

topics.title: Cold Outreach: Email & Cold Calling
topics.description: Write cold emails and make cold calls that earn a reply instead of getting ignored or hung up on.

steps.d: Draft a cold email that mentions something specific about the prospect (their product, their market, a recent announcement) and leads with why you're calling.
Send your template to ten warm contacts (people willing to help) and ask what it makes them want to do — click, reply, or delete.
Based on feedback, rewrite the email to lead with one specific value or insight and remove anything that sounds generic or pitchy.
Write a 30-second opening for a cold call that names one reason you called (not a pitch) and a specific ask (five-minute call next week).
Record your cold call script and listen back, noting pauses, speed, and whether you sound like a person or a script — re-record twice.

topics.title: Qualification Frameworks: BANT & MEDDIC
topics.description: Use BANT and MEDDIC to judge whether an opportunity is real and worth pursuing before investing more time in it.

steps.t: Identify Budget in a prospect conversation
steps.d: Ask 'What budget range did your team allocate for solving this problem?' and note whether it's set, flexible, or undecided — use that to gauge urgency and commitment.
Ask 'Who else needs to sign off on this decision?' and 'What's their approval process?' to understand whether you're talking to the decision-maker or influencer.

steps.t: Surface the actual Need they stated
steps.d: Restate the top three problems they mentioned in your discovery call and ask 'If we could fix these three, would that solve your core issue?' to confirm you nailed the need.
Ask 'When do you need this solved by?' and 'What happens if you don't implement anything?' to determine whether they'll close this quarter or you're in a long sales cycle.
After your discovery call, score each BANT component on a 1-5 scale; only move to a demo if Budget and Authority are 4-5 and Need is clearly linked to your solution.

topics.title: Running a Discovery Call
topics.description: Structure a discovery call so it uncovers a prospect's real pain points instead of just checking boxes.

steps.d: Write a discovery call agenda with four to five sections: rapport, problem understanding, impact, decision process.
Write five open-ended questions that surface the prospect's actual pain points (not yes-or-no questions), starting with how they currently solve the problem.
Run an actual discovery call with a prospect or qualified lead, record it (with permission) or take detailed notes of what they said about their challenges.
From the call notes, write down what the prospect actually said their pain point is versus what you thought it would be before the call.

steps.t: Plan next steps based on pain
steps.d: Decide whether to move forward and what you'd show or propose next, based on the actual pain point you uncovered (not on a generic demo).

topics.title: Active Listening & Questioning Techniques
topics.description: Listen and ask questions in a way that makes prospects actually open up about what they need.

steps.d: In your next call, hold silence for five seconds after the prospect finishes speaking before you respond (actually count) and write down what they said in that silence.
After a prospect describes a challenge, ask three follow-ups ('Tell me more', 'What happens when that occurs', 'How is that affecting you') instead of moving to your pitch.
Listen for what the prospect is NOT saying — budget concerns, competition worries, execution risk — and name one as a question: 'I'm guessing budget could be a factor.'.
When a prospect uses specific language to describe their problem, repeat it back in your next sentence using their exact words, not your terminology.
After three calls, ask a peer to score how much of each call was you talking versus the prospect talking — aim for 30% you, 70% them.

topics.title: SPIN Selling & Needs Analysis
topics.description: Use the SPIN question sequence to help a buyer connect their problem to the cost of leaving it unsolved.

steps.d: Study what SPIN questions are: Situation (open context), Problem (surface needs), Implication (impact), Need Payoff (demonstrate value).
For your product, write two questions per category (Situation, Problem, Implication, Need Payoff) that would help a buyer connect their problem to the cost of leaving it unsolved.
Role-play a sales call with a colleague where you ask only SPIN questions and they play the prospect — record or note where you jumped to your pitch too early.
Use SPIN questions in a real discovery call with a qualified prospect and write down the three biggest impacts they admitted.
In your next call with the same prospect, reference one of those impacts and describe how your product addresses it before showing a demo.

topics.title: Sales Presentations & Product Demos
topics.description: Tailor a demo to what a specific buyer cares about instead of running the same generic walkthrough every time.

steps.d: Before a demo, spend 15 minutes learning what this specific prospect's top challenge is (from their website, from the discovery call, or from someone who knows them).
Sketch a demo walkthrough that shows only the capabilities that address that prospect's top challenge, not a feature-by-feature tour.
In the demo, spend the first three minutes explaining how your product changes their workflow or results, before showing a single screen.
Give the demo to the prospect, asking them to try a key interaction themselves (don't watch) and observe where they engage or disengage.
After the demo, write down one part of your standard pitch that this prospect didn't care about and one question they asked that you didn't prepare for.

topics.title: Handling Objections
topics.description: Respond to price, fit, and competitor objections in a way that builds trust instead of triggering a debate.

steps.d: Write down the three to five objections you hear most often (price, fit, already have something, timing) and what you usually say in response.
When a prospect says 'it's too expensive', ask 'What would make it feel like a fair investment' instead of defending your price.
For each common objection, write a response that listens first, isolates the real concern, and then presents an option instead of arguing.
In your next sales call, when an objection comes up, pause and ask a question to dig into the real worry before responding.
After five calls where objections came up, note which ones moved the prospect forward and which ones remained blockers — what was different about your response.

topics.title: Value Selling & ROI Communication
topics.description: Translate your solution into the numbers a buyer's boss will actually approve.

steps.d: For one customer segment, calculate the tangible value your product creates: time saved, revenue gained, or cost reduced, with specific numbers.
Build a simple spreadsheet where you plug in their numbers (users, volume, current cost) and show the annual benefit of using your product.
Take three key features and for each write a simple sentence connecting it to business value: 'This reduces manual work by 20 hours per week, which costs them Z dollars per year'.
In a closing conversation, walk through your ROI model with a prospect and ask whether the value you're showing matches what they'd see.
Based on what the prospect said, update your ROI model with their actual data and show them the revised benefit using their numbers.

topics.title: Closing Techniques
topics.description: Recognize buying signals and use the right closing approach to move a ready deal to a signature.

steps.t: Recognize buying signals in the prospect's questions
steps.d: Note when they shift from problem discussion to implementation questions ('How long would deployment take?', 'How does billing work?') — these signal genuine buying intent.

steps.t: Summarize their approval and move them forward
steps.d: Use a summary close: 'Just to confirm, you need X solved by date Y, and you're ready to start implementation?'— then ask the exact next step (demo date, contract review, budget approval).

steps.t: Handle hesitation and uncover real concerns
steps.d: Respond to hesitation with 'What would help you decide?' not silence; uncover the real concern — price, fit, risk, timing — and address only that one rather than re-pitching.
Mention genuine reasons to close soon ('Our implementation team has availability next week') not artificial deadlines ('This pricing expires Friday') — real urgency builds trust.

steps.t: Get commitment to a specific next step
steps.d: Never end a call without agreement on the next action: 'You'll send me the tech requirements by Thursday and I'll send a proposal by Friday' — use a date and person/action, not 'let's stay in touch'.

topics.title: Sales Negotiation Fundamentals
topics.description: Negotiate price and terms without giving away margin for free or damaging the relationship.

steps.d: Set your opening number at least 10% higher than your ideal close price so there's room to negotiate and the prospect feels they won — don't open at your bottom line.

steps.t: Assess their price constraints before pushing
steps.d: Ask 'What budget range makes sense for you?' and listen to their answer; if it's far from your price, don't waste time negotiating — address fit concerns instead.
When they push back on price, don't just drop it — ask 'If I can move on price, would you commit to a three-year deal?' or 'Would you be ready to sign this week?' — trade concessions for commitments.

steps.t: Defend your price with value, not emotion
steps.d: Don't say 'That's my best price' — instead say 'Here's the ROI you'll see' or 'Here's what's included that your current provider doesn't have' to justify the number.
Before negotiations, calculate your actual minimum (cost + margin) and commit to it; don't let pressure erode that floor — it's the one number you will not move below.

topics.title: Sales Pipeline & CRM Fundamentals
topics.description: Keep a pipeline organized in a CRM so deals move forward instead of quietly going cold.

steps.d: Use your company's CRM to create a pipeline view showing every prospect by stage (prospecting, discovery, demo, negotiation, closed-won).
For each deal, log what you did (email, call, demo) and what happened (they said yes, they said maybe, they didn't respond) within one business day.
Every Friday, look at your pipeline and write down which deals are on track, which are stalled, and which you'll lose if you don't act this week.
Measure your conversion rates between stages (what % of prospects in discovery move to demo, what % of demos close) and compare to previous quarters.
Look at your pipeline data and identify which stage is your bottleneck (where most deals get stuck) and spend next week unblocking one stalled deal.

topics.title: Account Management Fundamentals
topics.description: Manage a portfolio of existing accounts so relationships and revenue grow instead of just being maintained.

steps.d: Categorize your current customers into three tiers by revenue or strategic importance and assign relationship priorities to each tier.
For three accounts in your portfolio, write down their current challenges, your last three interactions, and what they'd need to expand or renew.
Schedule a quarterly business review with one key account where you discuss their progress, ROI, and goals for the next quarter.
For each of your three accounts, list three potential upsells or features they're not using that could create more value for them.
For one strategic account, create a one-page plan documenting their goals, challenges, your expansion plays, and quarterly milestones to hit.

topics.title: Renewals & Customer Success
topics.description: Plan for renewal well before the contract ends by tracking account health and proving value along the way.

steps.d: For renewal-stage accounts, define three metrics that predict whether they'll renew: product usage, support tickets, engagement with your team.
For each account, schedule the renewal conversation at least 120 days before the contract ends and document what value you'll need to demonstrate.
For one account coming up for renewal, create a quarterly business review that shows the value they got: time saved, revenue gained, or problems solved.
When a renewal comes up, discuss price and terms (length, support level) early and write down what concessions you might make to secure the renewal.
Create a list of all renewals due in the next 12 months and categorize by risk (high risk to lose, medium, low) based on their product usage and engagement.

topics.title: Expansion Revenue & Upselling
topics.description: Grow revenue from existing customers through upsells and cross-sells that genuinely fit their needs.

steps.d: For each existing customer, list three ways revenue could grow: additional users, upgraded features, new products or add-ons they could buy.
Pick one customer and estimate their maximum possible annual value if they used all your products and all seats, then compare to current revenue.
Look at your product suite and identify which products are typically bought together — use that pattern to identify expansion for each customer segment.
Contact one customer who isn't using a relevant feature or product and propose it with one specific reason why it would help them.
After one quarter of expansion focus, calculate the percentage of revenue growth that came from new customers versus expansion from existing customers.
